4. The Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 is a law relating to the landlord and the tenant. East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was promulgated for the acquisition by the State of the interest of the rent-receivers and certain other interest in land and "to define the law relating to tenancies to be held under the State after such a acquisition and other matters connected herewith". Part- V of the Act mainly deals with the rights and obligations of agricultural tenants which was so long controlled and regulated under the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act and came in to force in different areas at different points of time, the earliest being 5-8-54 in the Subdivision of Patuakhali and the last being 5-8 65 in the District of Faridpur. 

 5. Section 26G was introduced by amending Act IV of 1982 which came into force on 22-2-29. The object of the legislature was to protect a raiyat "so that no mahajan can keep a raiyat out of his land for more than 15 years at the most" in return for a, petty loan. This section permitted an occupancy raiyat to create a complete unfructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 15 years and did not allow him to create any unfructuary mortgage as defined in section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act but the amending Act Of the Bengal Tenancy Act introduced a new definition of "complete unfructuary mortgage" by section 3(3), which says complete unfructuary mortgage means of transfer by a tenant of the right of possession in any land for the advanced or to be advanced by way of loan upon the condition that the loan with all interests thereon shall be deemed to be extinguished by the profit arising from the land during the period of mortgage". Under this sub-section the gradual process of reduction may not follow the strict rules of arithmetic. In other words no question of accounting arises unless an earlier redemption is proposed as contemplated by section 26G(2). It envisages automatic extinction of the loan both principal and interest within the stipulated period no matter whether the profits of land taken by the mortgagee had been of sufficient value to cover the total amount of the loan with interest thereon. The legal effect of it is that after expiry of the stipulated period the property automatically comes back to the mortgagor and the maximum period allowed by law was 15 years. The effect is that no unfructuary mortgage of the raiyati holding when even created can endure for a longer period than 15 years and they will be statutorily redeemed. Registration of documents creating a complete unfructuary mortgage for exceeding 15 years or unfructuary mortgage other than complete unfructuary mortgage was also forbidden and such documents were declared inadmissible in evidence., Thus a drastic change was made by Act IV of 1928 and a new type of mortgage being "complete unfructuary mortgage" was brought as a concept for the benefit of the raiyat. Litigations cropped up as to the retrospectively of his amendment and by Act IV of 1928, the legislature introduced section 26G(1) (a) and declared that every unfructuary mortgage created before 22-2-29 and which was subsisting on or after 1-8-38 (date of the commencement of the amendment) was to be deemed to be a complete unfructuary mortgage for period mentioned in the instrument or 15 years whichever is Jess. Sub-sections (5) and (6) were also inserted by Act VI of 1938 whereby it was provided that after the expiry of the period mentioned in the instrument or 15 years from the date of registration of the compete unfructuary mortgage or from the date of mortgagee’s entering into possession, as the case may be whichever is earlier, a complete unfructuary mortgage or an unfructuary mortgage sha1l be deemed to have been extinguished and the mortgagor there after would on application made either to civil court or revenue court be restored to possession. The Calcutta High Court in a number of decisions held that anomalous mortgage with possession given to the mortgagee, namely mortgage by conditional sale when the mortgagee had entered into possession was not covered by sub-section r) (a) and (5) [Badsha Mia Vs. Mobarrak Ali. 50 C. W.N. 578). Thereafter by amending Act XVIII of 1940 obviously for nullifying those decisions section 260 was further amended which provides that every form of mortgage executed before 22.2.29 and subsisting on or after 1.8.37 was to be deemed complete unfructuary mortgage if possession had been delivered to the mortgagee including a mortgage by conditional sale." The sub-section thus included a1l mortgages executed before 22.2.29 whether unfructuary or "anomalous" provided they were subsisting on 1-8-37 and as regards mortgages executed after the Act of 1928 it came to embrace all such mortgages whether "complete" unfructuary mortgage or "anomalous" mortgage provided they were executed before the Act 1940 and subsisting after the commencement of that Act. Sub-section (4) which created a bar against registration of documents creating unfructuary mortgage for more than 15 years or unfructuary mortgage other than complete unfructuary mortgage now added the "anomalous mortgage" to the list. Thus it is apparent by the amending Acts of 1928 and 1940 the legislature relieved the raiyat from all sorts of mortgages, namely (a) unfructuary mortgage. (b)a mortgage by conditional sale and (C) anomalous mortgages which are known concepts of the Transfer of Property Act. The raiyat can only create a complete unfructuary mortgage for which the definition was supplied by the Amending Act IV of 1928. It is not necessary to consider the incidents of unfructuary mortgage and mortgage by conditional sale or anomalous mortgage which are mentioned in section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act. The law extricated the raiyat from those mortgages and laid down that he can only create a complete unfructuary mortgage which is to be valid for a period not exceeding 15 years after which such mortgage is extinguished and on application before the Civil Court or revenue court his possession is restored. Then came East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (E.B. Act XXVIII of 1951). All the rent receiving interest were acquired with effect from 14-4-56 Section 95 of the Act provided that a raiyat could not enter into any form of unfructuary mortgage other than the complete unfructuary mortgage and every such complete unfructuary mortgage is subject to the limitation of section 90. Section 2(b) defined complete unfructuary mortgage which means a transfer by a tenant of the right of possession in any land for the purpose of securing the payment of money on the return of grain advanced or to be advanced by way of loan upon the condition that the loan with all interest thereon, shall be deemed to be extinguished by the profits ensuing from the land during the period of the mortgage".
